# Text as Data: tidytext {#sec-textasdata}

## Chapter objectives {.unnumbered}
In this chapter, you will learn how to use tidytext to treat 'text as data':

+ Using `unnest_tokens` to 'tokenize' a text, turning textual data into a tidy data frame with one word per row (@sec-textasdata-tokenization)
+ Analysing that data frame to show which words occur (@sec-textasdata-corpus)
+ Comparing two corpora (text collections) to highlight typical terms (@sec-textasdata-corpuscomparison)
+ Finding and using n-grams (word pairs or short phrases; @sec-textasdata-ngrams)
+ Using and validating dictionaries for document filtering and sentiment analysis (@sec-textasdata-dictionary)
+ Using LDA Topic Modeling to cluster words into topics (@sec-textasdata-topicmodeling)

As always, the chapter ends with a [multiple choice quiz](#sec-textasdata-quizquestions) organized per section that you can use to test your knowledge and understanding. You can also expand the table below to see which functions are covered in this chapter. 


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Functions introduced in this chapter"}

| Function | What it does | Section |
|:-----|:----------|:-----|
| `unnest_tokens()` | split a text column into tokens (words), with one row per token | @sec-textasdata-tokenization |
| `stop_words`, `get_stopwords()` | stop word lists, as data frames with a `word` column | @sec-textasdata-corpus |
| `bind_log_odds()` | add the weighted log odds of each word per corpus (from `tidylo`) | @sec-textasdata-corpuscomparison |
| `unnest_tokens(token="ngrams", n=)` | split a text column into n-grams rather than single words | @sec-textasdata-ngrams |
| `sentiments` | the Bing sentiment dictionary, as a data frame with a `word` column | @sec-textasdata-dictionary |
| `cast_sparse()` | turn a tidy token data frame into a (sparse) document-term matrix | @sec-textasdata-topicmodeling |
| `LDA()` | fit an LDA topic model (from `topicmodels`) | @sec-textasdata-topicmodeling |
| `posterior()` | get the word-topic (`terms`) and document-topic (`topics`) weights from a topic model | @sec-textasdata-topicmodeling |
| `reorder_within()`, `scale_y_reordered()` | order bars within each facet of a faceted plot | @sec-textasdata-topicmodeling |

:::

## Data for this chapter {.unnumbered}

For this chapter we will make use of the 'PImPo' (Parties' Immigration and Integration Positions) dataset [@lehmann2018;@lehmann2018ejpr], which is part of the [Manifesto Project](https://manifesto-project.wzb.eu/) [@lehmann2015]. 
The sample used in this chapter contains about 3,100 English and German sentences 
from political party manifestos that have been hand-coded for immigration and integration policy positions:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['pimpo_table', 'demo_tokenize', 'demo_contrast', 'demo_tokenize_chinese', 'demo_tokenize_examples', 'demo_word_counts', 'demo_stopwords', 'demo_stopwords_removed', 'demo_compare_proportion', 'demo_custom_stopwords', 'demo_bigrams', 'demo_bigrams_pmi']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
immigration_words <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic == "immigration", direction != "neutral") |>
  unnest_tokens(output=word, input=text) |>
  select(id, year, party_abbrev, direction, word)
```


```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/pimpo.csv", "pimpo.csv")
pimpo <- read_csv("pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
head(pimpo)
```

Since many analyses are language specific, 
we also created an English language subset `pimpo_en`
to make it a bit easier to work only on one language. 

Let's have a look at the distribution over topics and directions per country:

```{webr}
#| exercise: pimpo_table
pimpo |> 
  count(topic, direction, country) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from=country, values_from=n)
```

As you can see, about half of the sentences are about immigration or integration,
and all of these are coded for the position of that party on the topic. 

Note that this dataset is a small sample of the full Manifesto and PImPo datasets,
redistributed with permission from the Manifesto Project. 
The full dataset can be obtained using the [manifestoR](https://manifesto-project.wzb.eu/manifestor) package,
see [this page](https://manifesto-project.wzb.eu/information/documents/pimpo) for instructions on how to get an API key and download the data,
and see [our data folder README](https://github.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/blob/main/data/README.md) for the script we used to prepare it. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Columns in the PImPo data - click to expand

| Variable            | Type          | Explanation                                                                                        |
|---------------------|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| id                  | numeric (dbl) | Unique number of each sentence in the original PImPo data                                          |
| country             | character     | Country of the party (Australia, Austria, Ireland, or United States)                               |
| year                | numeric (dbl) | Year of the election for which the manifesto was written (1999–2013)                               |
| party               | character     | Name of the party, as given by the Manifesto Project                                               |
| party_abbrev        | character     | Abbreviated party name                                                                             |
| text                | character     | The text of the (quasi-)sentence                                                                   |
| topic               | character     | Whether the sentence is about `immigration`, `integration`, or neither (`other`)                   |
| direction           | character     | Position towards immigration or integration: `supportive`, `neutral`, or `sceptical` (missing if the topic is `other`) |
| certainty_topic     | numeric (dbl) | Percentage of coders who agreed on the topic (missing if the topic is `other`)                     |
| certainty_direction | numeric (dbl) | Percentage of coders who agreed on the direction (missing if the topic is `other`)                 |

Note that in the full manifestos data set, only a couple percent of sentences are about immigration or integration.
This data set consists of all those sentences (n=1,548) and an equal number of 
randomly drawn sentences not about immigration or integration,
so exactly 50% of each country's sentences is about immigration/integration.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Using your own data with readtext"}

The examples in this book all use ready-made csv files available through the Internet.
There is a good chance, however, that you might want to analyse text files that are on your own computer. 

By far the easiest way to read in multiple text files is using the `readtext` package. You can point this package at a folder (or zip file) and it will automatically read all files inside it. Even better, it automatically parses pdf and docx files and turns them into plain text columns:

```r
> readtext("your_folder_or_zipfile") |> as_tibble()
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  doc_id             text                    
  <chr>              <chr>                   
1 plaintext.txt      "A normal text file"    
3 word_file.docx     "Text from a .docx file"
4 document.pdf       "Text from a pdf file"
```

See @sec-readtext (coming soon!) for more details on reading data into R.
:::

## `unnest_tokens`: From characters to words {#sec-textasdata-tokenization}

In the previous chapter we have used regular expressions to do text analysis,
but this is sometimes awkward as we are normally interested in words rather than characters.
Using the `tidytext` package, we can `unnest` a text and create a row for each word.
For example, this creates a data frame with all the words used to talk about
immigration by the English-language manifestos:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_tokenize
library(tidytext)
immigration_words <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic == "immigration", direction != "neutral") |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |> 
  select(id, year, party_abbrev, direction, word)
head(immigration_words)
```

<!-- TODO: I use unnest_tokens(text, output=word), which to me is most natural conventional tidy. However, unnest_tokens(word, text) is probably the more common form. Keep, swith to that, or use unnest_tokens(input=text, output=word)? -->

Since this is just a normal data frame, we can use regular tidyverse functions
to do analysis. 
For example, let's plot the most contrasting words used for each position:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_contrast
immigration_words |>
  count(word, direction) |>
  group_by(word) |>
  mutate(n_total=sum(n), proportion=n/n_total) |>
  filter(n_total > 5) |> arrange(desc(proportion)) |>
  group_by(direction) |>
  slice_max(order_by=proportion, n=10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=proportion, y=fct_reorder(word, proportion), fill=direction)) + 
    geom_col() + 
    facet_wrap(vars(direction), scales = "free_y") + 
    theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position="none") +
    labs(title="Typical words in positions supportive or sceptical of migration", 
         caption="Data: PImPo (Lehmann & Zobel 2018), sentences from AU, US, IE",
         x="", y="")
```


As you can see, sentences that express skepticism towards immigration in this sample
talk about aliens and use words such as enter, boats, borders, rule and enforcement. 
Sentences supportive of immigration instead talk about refugees using words like rights, needs, family/families, and comprehensive reform. 

Looking at the code, it might look complex at first but it really only uses the tidyverse
building blocks you mastered in earlier chapters, especially @sec-summarize.
First, we compute the `count` of each word per direction (stance)
and in total. Next, we compute the proportion of each word in that direction, showing us whether a word is almost exclusively used in that direction (proportion near 1) or used as much regardless of the direction (proportion near the total percentage of words in that direction). 
We can then `filter` to only keep words with more than five mentions,
and use `slice_max` to select only the ten words that have the highest proportion per direction. 
Finally, we make a bar chart of the top words (@sec-vis), using `facet_wrap` to create separate facets for sceptical and supportive words (@sec-vis-facets).

::: {.callout-tip title="Tokenization in detail"}

Even the simple example above already shows the benefits of working with words instead of character strings. 
Questions such as which words are used or overused become simple tidyverse operations.
However, as the example above shows, words that seem similar such as "family" and "families" are treated as distinct words, while "Australia's" is seen as a single word.

This shows that it is important to understand a bit better what's going on under the hood. 
The process of turning text (a string of characters) into words is called *tokenization*,
with words often referred to as *tokens* in language processing.
The `unnest_tokens` function above is quite powerful and can deal with different languages,
including languages like Chinese or Japanese that don't use spaces to mark word boundaries:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_tokenize_chinese
tibble(text="为人民服务") |> unnest_tokens(text, output=word)
```

As the example above shows, Mao's call to "serve the people" is correctly
tokenized into 为 ("for"), 人民 ("the people"), and 服务 ("serve"). 

Tokenization, however, is not a one-size-fits-all operation. 
Let's look at some more examples:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_tokenize_examples
tibble(text = c("1:30 to go 🙏 #ge2024 #ireland",
                "Sinn Féin's vice-president",
                "https://r4css.vanatteveldt.com",              
                "verhinderung von Kettenasylantragstellungen")) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word, drop = FALSE, strip_punct=FALSE) |> 
  group_by(text) |>
  summarize(tokens = str_c(word, collapse="🔹"))
```

As these examples show, tokenization depends strongly on the presence of spaces and punctuation, although it does not blindly split on all punctuation. 
As you can see, both `1:30` and `#ge2024` are split into multiple tokens,
which is probably not how we would normally see it. 
In the next text, `Sinn Féin` is split into two tokens, with the possessive s in `Féin's` seen as part of the token. 
In the url below it, the `://` part is seen as three distinct tokens, while the domain name is kept as a single token.
Finally, the beautiful German compound Kettenasylantragstellungen ("chain asylum applications") is seen as a single word. 

In each case, the tokenization is correct (or at least defensible).
However, it does show that in analyses you need to pay attention to tokenization issues:
for example, a naive search for asylum applications in German would miss that compound,
and similarly looking for Sinn Féin or the use of hyperlinks after tokenization would be hard.
All of these issues can be addressed by preprocessing and/or more careful morphological analysis, but make sure that you check the outcome of your tokenization to make sure that what you would call a word or term is also what comes out of `unnest_tokens`. 

Note finally in the code that we first use `unnest_tokens` to create a long data frame,
and then use `summarize` to collapse all the tokens of each sentence back to a single text, with a distinctive marker between the tokens. 
:::

## Corpus Analysis {#sec-textasdata-corpus}

Let's have a closer look at the PImPo *corpus* (corpus being the fancy word linguists use when they mean a collection of texts). 

Which words are used to discuss immigration?

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_word_counts
pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic == "immigration") |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  count(word) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

Although this is a literal answer to our question, it is not a very informative one:
in almost any text words like "the"  and "to" would be in the top of this list.

### Stop words

Such words are called 'stop words', i.e. words that should be "stopped" from entering the analysis. 
Various stop word lists exist for most languages, and for English a selection of stop word lists is immediately available as `stop_words` data frame:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_stopwords
print("English stop words from `stop_words`")
stop_words

print("Using the stopwords package to get a list for other languages")
get_stopwords("de", source="stopwords-iso")
```

Since these stopword lists are data frames with a 'word' column, 
we can directly use `anti_join` to remove them from our analysis:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_stopwords_removed
pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic == "immigration") |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  anti_join(stop_words) |>
  count(word) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

And the result is clearly much more informative, with "immigration", "asylum" and "seekers" forming the top three. 

::: {.challenge title="German words"}
Can you adapt the code above to give the list of most frequent words for the Austrian sentences?
:::

### Corpus comparison {#sec-textasdata-corpuscomparison}

It is often very informative to *compare* word use in two corpora.
As in the opening example of the chapter, we can see which words are used
more in sceptical relative to supportive statements about immigration.
We could also investigate whether US party manifestos use different words to talk about immigration than Irish, or whether immigration vocabulary changed over time. 

Let's start by looking at the proportion of each word's usage in Irish manifesto sentences about integration or immigration:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_compare_proportion
immigration_vocabulary <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic %in% c("immigration", "integration"), 
         country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |> 
  count(country, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=country, values_from=n, values_fill=0) |>
  rename(ie=Ireland, us="United States") 

immigration_vocabulary |>
  mutate(total=ie+us, prop_ie=ie / total) |>
  filter(total>10) |>
  arrange(desc(prop_ie))
```

This produces some interesting findings: apparently asylum and employment
are uniquely Irish concerns in the immigration manifestoes. 
Unsurprisingly, it also contains a lot of words referring to Ireland and the EU. 
If you change the last line to `arrange(prop_ie)` you will see that in the US discourse
even more of the top-10 words refer to the nation.

However, this comparison is very naive. 
First, we did not do any cleaning (although `unnest_tokens` by default lowercases and removes punctuation).
Proportion as a measure is also deeply flawed: 
it does not take into account that the Irish corpus is simply bigger than the American
(probably because they have more parties, even though there are three US election cycles in the data versus only two Irish ones).
Moreover, since proportion peaks at 1 when only one corpus uses a word,
it will show mostly which words are unique, even if there are much more frequent words that are overused in either corpus. 
This is mitigated a bit by setting a minimum frequency (`total>10`), 
but that is an arbitrary cutoff value. 

For the cleaning, this is actually a case where stopword removal probably will do more harm than good: 
comparison naturally filters out words that are very frequent in both corpora, 
and if US parties use 'should' more while Irish parties use 'will' more (which they actually do!), this might be an interesting finding rather than noise. 
However, two cleaning steps are probably a good idea: 
removing the possessive `'s`, and creating a manual 'stop word list' containing country and party names. 

To create the manual list, we can actually use the `party` column for the party names,
using `unnest_tokens` again to separate the parties into words:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_custom_stopwords
country_words <- tibble(word=c("ireland", "irish", "america", "american", "americans", "united", "states"))
party_words <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  select(party) |>
  unnest_tokens(input = party, output = word) |>
  distinct() 
custom_stopwords <- bind_rows(country_words, party_words)
custom_stopwords$word
```

This also shows how stop words are often not a trivial decision:
as the list includes 'united', 'fine' and 'left', it would remove these words regardless of whether they are used as party names.
This can partly be solved by postponing the lower casing until after using the stop word list, but e.g. 'Left' could also be used as the start of a sentence so it won't fully solve it. Using word combinations ("n-grams") would be a better solution here, see @sec-textasdata-ngrams below. 

A classical measure in corpus comparison is *chi-squared*,
which is a standard non-parametric statistic that we can use to test whether
a country uses a word more (or less) frequently than 'expected', i.e. than if usage were unrelated to country. 
Although this is an oft-used measure, it overestimates the unexpectedness for rare words
(and paradoxically, in language rare words are very common!)

For this reason, @monroe08 suggest using a weighted log-odds measure which they demonstrate
by comparing Republican and Democratic word use on issues such as abortion.
The log-odds ratio essentially tells us how much less surprised we would be to encounter a word if we know whether it came from the Irish or American corpus. 
It is also the same statistic used in logistic regression to indicate 
how strongly the independent variable (country) is related to the dependent variable (is it this word or a different word).
This measure is then smoothed to deal with low frequency words, 
and weighted by dividing by the standard error to produce something akin to a z-score. 
The good news is that this measure is implemented in the `tidylo` package,
so we don't need to know any mathematics to be able to use it. 

Let's put these steps together and get a more well-founded corpus comparison:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_compare_logodds', 'demo_compare_plot']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(tidylo)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")

country_words <- tibble(word=c("ireland", "irish", "america", "american", "americans", "united", "states"))
party_words <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  select(party) |>
  unnest_tokens(input = party, output = word) |>
  distinct()
custom_stopwords <- bind_rows(country_words, party_words)

immigration_comparison <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(country %in% c("United States", "Ireland"),
         topic %in% c("immigration", "integration")) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  mutate(word = str_remove(word, "['’]s$")) |>
  anti_join(custom_stopwords, by = "word") |>
  count(country, word) |>
  complete(country, word, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  mutate(n_other = sum(n) - n, .by = word) |>
  bind_log_odds(country, word, n)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_compare_logodds
library(tidylo)
immigration_comparison <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic %in% c("immigration", "integration"),
         country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  mutate(word = str_remove(word, "['’]s$")) |>
  anti_join(custom_stopwords) |>
  count(country, word)  |> 
  complete(country, word, fill = list(n = 0)) |> 
  mutate(n_other = sum(n) - n, .by=word) |>
  bind_log_odds(country, word, n)

immigration_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(log_odds_weighted))
```

As you can see from this output, the words that are found are quite different from the words in the earlier (proportion-based) list. 
The weighted log odds focuses less on the words that were exclusive to either corpus (for which proportion=1) and more on more common words that are overused in either corpus. 
For example, take *our* in the American manifestos: it is also used in the Irish manifestos, so its proportion is much lower than 1 and it didn't show up in the first results above. But because it's a very common word, a difference this large is much less likely to be due to chance, making it the top word by weighted log odds. 
Arguably, overused common words are substantively more interesting than less frequent exclusive words, but of course that ultimately depends on the research question. 

Besides this substantive difference, the statistical measure also avoids the need for an arbitrary frequency cutoff, gives a more informative measure of the 'keyness' of each word, and solves the problem of not accounting for the relative size of both corpora.

Looking at the code, most of it should start looking familiar.
We start by filtering and tokenizing as above. 
Then we have two cleaning steps, removing all word-ending `'s` and removing words from our custom stop word list.
Then we count the frequency of each word in each corpus, 
and use `complete` to ensure words not used in a corpus get a zero
(which is necessary for computing the log odds ratio correctly).
Then we add two additional columns:
`n_other` so we can compare frequencies more easily (using `.by=` as a shortcut for `group_by`), and `bind_log_odds` to add the log odds column.

Finally, let's use this to create a graph similar to those used in @monroe08, with word frequency on the horizontal axis and keyness on the vertical:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_compare_plot
all_words <- immigration_comparison |>
  filter(country == "United States") |>
  mutate(x = n + n_other + runif(n(), -.4, .4))

focus_words <- all_words |> 
  filter(abs(log_odds_weighted) > .8 | n+n_other > 100) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(log_odds_weighted)))

ggplot(all_words, aes(x=x, y=log_odds_weighted)) + 
  geom_hline(lty=2, color="grey", yintercept=0) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) + 
  geom_text(data=focus_words, aes(label=word, color=log_odds_weighted),
            check_overlap = TRUE,size = 3.5, vjust = -0.5) + 
  scale_color_gradient2(low="#2ca25f", high="#1f4e9c", mid="#444", midpoint=0, guide=NULL) + 
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000)) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) + 
  labs(title="Which words are used in US and Irish manifestos to talk about immigration?",
       subtitle="(Words with identical counts are spread out horizontally)",
       caption="Data: PImPo (Lehmann & Zobel 2018)",
       x="Word frequency (log scale)", 
       y="Weighted log odds\n  ← Irish | American →")
```

This graph shows all words from the comparison, with words overused in American manifestos on the top (and in blue), and words used more in Ireland at the bottom in green. 
More common words are on the right and rare words on the left, 
with the horizontal 'bands' indicating how many words shared the same count and log odds value.

This graph nicely shows the different words used in both countries:
American manifestos talk about borders, law, illegal, aliens and immigrants and use 'our' and 'we' a lot; while Irish manifestos talk about asylum (seekers), integration, permits, and applications. 
On the right you can see that traditional stop words such as "in" or "and" have low log odds scores, making normal stop word removal unnecessary (and even harmful as it generally also removes words like 'our' or 'we').


<!-- 
Not sure whether to include something like this (with a reference to Zipf or power law distribution)
Finally the plot clearly shows that most of the words are in the center-left: 
there is a 'long tail' of words with low frequency that are not (statistically) typical for either corpus.
In most cases, the interesting words for analysis are neither the very rare ones nor the very frequent ones, as the latter tend to be 'stop words' like *and* and *the*.
-->

Looking at the code, there are a number of interesting "tricks" used to make this graph:

- First, we select the US words as main data set, and manually calculate the `x` position by adding some random noise to the total word frequency. We could also have used `geom_jitter`, but by adding the noise before the log transformation it has less effect on words with a higher count.
- Next, we define a separate set of 'focus words' to highlight, in this case taking all words with an absolute log odds of above .8 or a total frequency above 100. 
- In the ggplot, we use a regular `geom_point` to show all words as points, with a low alpha value to show overlapping points. A `hline` shows a dashed y=0 line as a visual guide. 
- Then, a `geom_text` with `data=focus_words` shows text only for the chosen words, using `vjust` to make sure the labels are shown above the points. 

The rest is fairly straightforward: a log x scale, a minimal theme, and labels to make the graph interpretable. 


::: {.callout-tip title="Preprocessing choices"}

The steps involved in cleaning or transforming a text before the analysis are generally called *preprocessing*. 
Although there are many steps that are commonly used, such as converting to lower case
and stripping punctuation, there is no agreed-on "recipe" that each analysis should use.
In fact, how you should preprocess depends on your research question [cf. @grimmer2022text]: 
if you are looking at social identity you probably want to keep *stop words* like "us" and "them", while a topical analysis probably wants to ignore those.

Below we list a table of the most common preprocessing steps, based loosely on the reviews by @denny2018text and @hickman2022text:

| Choice | Description | Method (or Code) |
|:-------|:------------|:-----------------|
| Lowercasing | Treat *Immigration* and *immigration* as the same word | On by default; turn off with `unnest_tokens(..., to_lower = FALSE)` |
| Punctuation and symbols | Remove tokens such as `:`, `#` or `-` (and emoji) | On by default; keep them with `unnest_tokens(..., strip_punct = FALSE)` |
| Numbers | Remove numeric tokens such as `1,500` | `unnest_tokens(..., strip_numeric = TRUE)` |
| Stop words | Remove frequent words with little content (*the*, *and*, *der*) | `anti_join(stop_words)`; for other languages `get_stopwords(language = "de")` |
| Trimming | Remove words that are too rare (or too common) to be informative | `add_count(word) |> filter(n >= 5)` |
| Stemming | Cut words back to a common stem (*families*, *family* → *famili*) | Provided by e.g. the `SnowballC` package |
| Lemmatization | Replace words by their dictionary form (*families* → *family*, *went* → *go*) | Provided by e.g. the `udpipe` or `spacyr` packages |
| n-grams | Use combinations of adjacent words as tokens (*sinn féin*, *not good*) | `unnest_tokens(..., token = "ngrams", n = 2)` |
| Negation | Keep track of negated words (*not good*) | Use bigrams, or join the negation to the next word before tokenizing |
| Spelling and abbreviations | Normalise variants (*U.S.*, *US*, *USA*) and spelling errors | Recode with `str_replace_all()` before tokenizing, or a spell checker such as `hunspell` |

:::

### Exercise: Sceptical or supportive?

{{< include exercises/_ch10_ex_compare_direction.qmd >}}

## Collocations and N-grams {#sec-textasdata-ngrams}

In the examples so far, we have focused on single words.
However, very often it is more informative to treat word combinations like `United states` or `rule of law` as a single token. 

To do this, we can use `unnest_tokens(token="ngrams")` to tokenize to n-grams rather than words. 
In language processing, an n-gram is a sequence of n words, so `United states` is a 2-gram (or bigram) and `rule of law` is a trigram. 


```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_bigrams
bigrams <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=token, token="ngrams", n=2) |>
  count(token) |>
  arrange(-n)
bigrams
```

As you can see, most bigrams are actually not that interesting, with patterns like "of the" and "in the" dominating the list. 

As before, this can be remedied relatively easily by removing stop words.
Of course, we cannot simply `anti_join` on the stop word list as the tokens are now bigrams,
but we can create a regular expression pattern for any ngrams that contain a bigram
by collapsing all stop words to a single `|`-separated pattern and placing `\\b` on either side:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: demo_bigrams_stopwords
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
bigrams <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=token, token="ngrams", n=2) |>
  count(token) |>
  arrange(-n)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_bigrams_stopwords
stop_words_pattern <- str_glue("\\b({str_c(stop_words$word, collapse='|')})\\b")
bigrams_filtered <- bigrams |>
  filter(!str_detect(token, stop_words_pattern))
bigrams_filtered
```

This is already a quite informative list, showing meaningful combinations like *asylum seekers* and party names like *fine gael*. 

However, as above stop words are a very blunt solution. 
For example, `united states` is not present above because the onix stop word list contains `states` as a stop word. On the other extreme, the smaller 'snowball' stop word list does not contain a word such as 'will', so switching to that list will bring in patterns like "will also".

In corpus linguistics, point-wise mutual information (PMI) is often used for detecting *collocations*: word combinations which are more frequent than you would expect from their underlying frequencies.
There is no built-in function for computing PMI in `tidytext`, but fortunately it is relatively easy to compute it ourselves:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_bigrams_pmi
word_freq <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=word) |>
  count(word, name="n_word") |>
  mutate(p_word=n_word / sum(n_word))

bigrams_pmi <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=bigram, token="ngrams", n=2) |>
  count(bigram) |>
  mutate(p_bigram=n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(n >= 5) |>
  unnest_tokens(input=bigram, output=word, drop=FALSE) |>
  left_join(word_freq, by = "word") |>
  summarize(pmi = log2(first(p_bigram)) - sum(log2(p_word)), n = first(n), .by = bigram) |>
  arrange(desc(pmi))

bigrams_pmi
```

Substantively, this list looks mostly right, with Irish party names topping the list as both fianna and fáil only occur as part of the collocation. 
It also contains terms like 'green card' and 'climate change', titles like 'president bush', and constructs like 'long term'. 
Most importantly, bigrams like 'of the' are not included:
Since stop words are themselves very frequent, combinations with stop words are expected to be relatively frequent as well.

### Using n-grams in frequency analysis

We can use the bigrams we found above to preprocess the texts before a regular frequency analysis.
In particular, we can create a list of replacements so e.g. "green party" becomes "green_party":

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_collocations', 'demo_compare_ngrams']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(tidylo)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")

word_freq <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=word) |>
  count(word, name="n_word") |>
  mutate(p_word=n_word / sum(n_word))

bigrams_pmi <- pimpo_en |>
  unnest_tokens(input=text, output=bigram, token="ngrams", n=2) |>
  count(bigram) |>
  mutate(p_bigram=n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(n >= 5) |>
  unnest_tokens(input=bigram, output=word, drop=FALSE) |>
  left_join(word_freq, by = "word") |>
  summarize(pmi = log2(first(p_bigram)) - sum(log2(p_word)), n = first(n), .by = bigram) |>
  arrange(desc(pmi))

collocations <- bigrams_pmi |> filter(pmi >= 8) |> pull(bigram)
replacements <- str_replace_all(collocations, " ", "_") |>
  set_names(str_glue("\\b{collocations}\\b"))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_collocations
collocations <- bigrams_pmi |> filter(pmi >= 8) |> pull(bigram)
replacements <- str_replace_all(collocations, " ", "_") |>
  set_names(str_glue("\\b{collocations}\\b"))
replacements
```

As you can see, this is a *named vector* of strings, where the name is the pattern to look for 
(`\\bunited states\\b`) and the value is the replacement (`united_states`). 
This is created by first selecting those bigrams with a pmi over 8 and 'pulling' the bigram column.
We then replace the spaces by underscores, and finally set the pattern as the names. 

This can be used to augment earlier analyses, e.g. the word comparison:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_compare_ngrams
pimpo_en |>
  filter(country %in% c("United States", "Ireland"),
         topic %in% c("immigration", "integration")) |>
  mutate(text=str_replace_all(str_to_lower(text), replacements)) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |> 
  count(country, word) |>
  complete(country, word, fill=list(n=0)) |>
  bind_log_odds(country, word, n) |>
  arrange(desc(log_odds_weighted)) 
```

As you can see, `united_states` is now seen as a single token, and (if you scroll down) so are terms like `asylum_seekers` and `illegal_aliens` and Irish parties like `fine_gael`.
Note that we call `str_replace_all` on the lowercased text, as our collocations are all lower cased. 

Note that we used the value 8 based on inspection of the bigrams,
as there is no sensible agreed-on cutoff value. 
Depending on the research question it can also be a good idea to manually curate this list to ensure
that e.g. all party names are included. 

## Dictionary Analysis {#sec-textasdata-dictionary}

One of the oldest tools in the computational social science toolbox is dictionary analysis:
using a (generally hand crafted) set of words to detect whether a concept occurs or to measure a variable such as tone or stance. 

### Topic classification {#sec-textasdata-topicdictionary}

As a first application of a dictionary, let's see if we can create a dictionary to classify
whether topics are relevant for a specific topic. 
In general, identifying relevant documents for analysis is an excellent use case for dictionaries.

In this case, we might want to know specifically whether a document is about migration. 
Although it is entirely possible (and sometimes the best idea) to create a dictionary yourself,
it is also a good idea to check the literature for existing dictionaries.
For example, @palicki2023selecting published an 'expert validated search query' for migration,
which we can use in a shortened form:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_dictionary_match', 'demo_dictionary_confusion', 'demo_precision_recall']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
immigration_pattern <- "asyl|immigra|migra|refugee|foreigner|emigra"
immigration_matches <- pimpo_en |>
  select(id, country, party, topic, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(input="text", output="word") |>
  mutate(immigration=str_starts(word, immigration_pattern))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_dictionary_match
immigration_pattern <- "asyl|immigra|migra|refugee|foreigner|emigra"
immigration_matches <- pimpo_en |> 
  select(id, country, party, topic, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(input="text", output="word") |>
  mutate(immigration=str_starts(word, immigration_pattern)) 
immigration_matches
```

As you can see, this created a new column `immigration`, which is `TRUE` if the word matched the dictionary and `FALSE` otherwise. 
To validate how well the dictionary works, we can summarize the output per sentence
and compare the dictionary output to the actual topic:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_dictionary_confusion
immigration_matches  |>
  summarize(immigration=any(immigration), .by=c(id, topic)) |>
  count(topic, immigration) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=immigration, values_from=n)
```

The resulting table is called a *confusion matrix*, with the gold standard outcomes in the rows,
and the classification predictions in the columns, and each cell showing the frequency of that combination. Note that we group by `c(id, topic)` -- since every sentence has a single topic, this doesn't actually affect the grouping compared to just grouping by `id`, but it means that the topic per sentence is preserved in the summarization result. 

The good news is that when the dictionary found a word (the `` `TRUE` `` column) the sentence was almost always about immigration or integration. 
The less good news is that many of the immigration and integration sentences were missed by the dictionary.


::: {.callout-tip title="Precision and recall"}
The pattern found above is fairly common in dictionaries: 
because so many different words can be used to refer to a topic, 
when there is a match it's likely to be relevant, but many relevant texts are missed. 

In text analysis, we often use the terms *precision* and *recall* to indicate these metrics:
Precision is the proportion of all matched items that were indeed relevant,
while recall is the proportion of actually relevant items that were matched. 

In the example above, if we consider immigration and integration to both be relevant,
we have 217+93=310 *true positives*: relevant items that were correctly identified.

To calculate precision, we compare this to the *false positives*, items that were incorrectly classified as relevant. Here we only found 2, so precision is 310/(310+2)=99%

For recall, we instead compare to the *false negatives*, items that were missed (i.e. incorrectly classified as irrelevant). In this case the dictionary missed 112+128=240 sentences, giving a recall of 310/(310+240)=56%.

We can also use `summarize` to calculate these:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_precision_recall
immigration_matches |>
  summarize(match = any(immigration), .by = c(id, topic)) |>
  mutate(relevant = topic != "other") |>
  summarize(precision = sum(relevant & match) / sum(match),
            recall = sum(relevant & match) / sum(relevant))
```

You can change `topic != "other"` to `topic == "immigration"` in the chunk above to calculate precision and recall if we would only consider immigration sentences as relevant.
As you can see, this increases recall at the expense of precision -- which makes sense given that the confusion matrix showed that the current dictionary also matches 93 integration sentences.
:::

{{< include exercises/_ch10_challenge_dictionary.qmd >}}

### Sentiment analysis

Dictionaries are frequently used in sentiment analysis, 
even though research often finds they perform poorly in social science applications [cf @vanatteveldt2021validity]. Let's see whether an existing dictionary can differentiate between sceptical and supportive sentences. 

Tidytext ships with the sentiment dictionary published by @huliu04 (often called the Bing dictionary after its second author's first name)

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_sentiment_dictionary', 'demo_sentiment_join', 'demo_sentiment_confusion']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
bing <- sentiments |>
  mutate(value = if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1))
immigration_sentiment <-  pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic != "other")|>
  select(id, country, party, topic, direction, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(output=word, input=text) |>
  left_join(bing, by="word")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_sentiment_dictionary
bing <- sentiments |>
  mutate(value = if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1))
bing
```

Since this dictionary contains full words instead of word stems, 
we can join it to the result of `unnest_tokens`:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_sentiment_join
immigration_sentiment <-  pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic != "other")|>
  select(id, country, party, topic, direction, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(output=word, input=text) |>
  left_join(bing) 
immigration_sentiment
```

As you can see, most words are not matched, resulting in `NA`s,
while the word `integrated` is actually coded as positive. 
Note that we need to use `left_join` here, as otherwise any sentences without matches
would be silently dropped from the dataset.

Let's sum the values per sentence, and see how they relate to the coded sentiment:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_sentiment_confusion
predictions <- immigration_sentiment |>
  summarize(value = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(id, direction)) |>
  mutate(predicted = case_when(value < 0 ~ "sceptical",
                               value > 0 ~ "supportive",
                               .default = "neutral")) 
predictions |>
  count(direction, predicted) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = predicted, values_from = n)
```

So, if we assume the sign of the summed sentiment values should correspond to the direction of the stance, this dictionary is performing quite poorly.
Overall accuracy is only 49%, performing even worse than just guessing 'supportive' for each sentence. 
Especially sceptical is problematic, with almost as many sceptical sentences coded as positive as negative. 
This is quite likely due to words that express a desire for stricter immigration and integration rules, 
but that are coded as positive. We saw the word integrated above, but also words like 'secure' and 'effective' are coded as positive in the dictionary.

## Topic Modeling {#sec-textasdata-topicmodeling}

This chapter so far has mostly looked at which words (and bigrams) occur in a document.
It can also be very informative to see which words *co-occur*:
can we find coherent clusters of words that often occur together?

Although we will go into this in much more detail in @sec-embeddings,
this section will give a small demo of *topic modeling*,
which used to be a very popular method for exploring a corpus
[@blei2003latent; see e.g. @jacobi2016quantitative for an application to political communication].

### The document-term matrix as a bag of words {#sec-textasdata-dtm}

Before running the actual topic model, we convert the 'long' format of the tokens
into a 'wide' format with one word in every column: a *document-term matrix* or DTM. 
Since this would produce thousands of columns with mostly zeroes in the cells, rather than using a regular `pivot_wider` we use `cast_sparse`. 
This creates a *sparse matrix* format to represent the DTM, 
which is an efficient way to store such a matrix as only the non-zero cells are actually stored.


```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_dtm', 'demo_lda']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
dtm <- pimpo_en |>
  select(id:party, text, topic) |>
  unnest_tokens(input="text", output="word") |>
  anti_join(stop_words) |>
  count(id, word) |>
  cast_sparse(row=id, column=word, value=n)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_dtm
dtm <- pimpo_en |>
  select(id:party, text, topic) |>
  unnest_tokens(input="text", output="word") |>
  anti_join(stop_words) |>
  count(id, word) |>
  cast_sparse(row=id, column=word, value=n)
str_glue("dtm is a {class(dtm)} with {nrow(dtm)} rows (docs) and {ncol(dtm)} columns (words)")
dtm[1:5, c(1, 8, 18, 20)]
```

Looking at the first 5 rows and a hand-picked set of columns shows the structure of the dtm: 
each row is a document, and every column is a word. 
The word *ensure* occurs only in document `193798`, but *social* occurs also in document `194040`.
This latter document also contains *anti* and *behaviour* (twice).
It is tempting to read this as `193798` talking about *ensuring* (something) *social*,
and `194040` as talking about *anti social behaviour*, but the DTM only tells us these words occur,
not in which order or context -- you would have to check the actual sentences to learn the usage and context. 
This is why a dtm is often called a 'bag of words': 
every document is represented as a set of word frequencies, but all ordering or syntactic structure is ignored. 

### Estimating the topic model {#sec-textasdata-lda}

We can use the `topicmodels` package to cluster this matrix into topics:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_lda
library(topicmodels)
t <- LDA(dtm, k=10, control=list(seed=99))

topic_terms <- posterior(t) |> 
  pluck("terms") |> 
  as_tibble(rownames = "lda_topic") |>
  pivot_longer(-lda_topic, names_to = "term", values_to = "beta") 

topic_terms |>
  slice_max(beta, n = 10, by = lda_topic) |>
  summarise(terms = str_c(term, collapse = ", "), .by = lda_topic)
```

This shows the top-10 words for each topic. 
A number of topics all seem related to immigration in different ways:
topics 1-3 all mention immigration prominently, but also mention specific countries (Ireland, Australia, and the US respectively).
Topic 5 talks about law enforcement and language, and topic 9 talks about asylum seekers.
Other topics are less directly immigration-related: 
topic 4 is about government services, while topic 7 talks about workers and emplotment and 10 about families and schools.
Note that it is not surprising that this corpus yields a mix of immigration and non-immigration topics, with a strong focus on immigration, as it was sampled to have 50% of sentences about immigration or integration. 

Looking at the code, we can see some interesting things:

- The LDA call creates a topic model `t` with `k=10` clusters. We set a random seed for reproducibility since topic modeling is non-deterministic.
- To analyse the results, we take the `posterior` distribution from the model, from which we `pluck` the "terms", which is a matrix of probabilities for each term within each topic (pluck is a helper function that takes an element from a list within a tidyverse pipeline)
- We convert this matrix to a tibble, and pivot it to a long format of weights ("betas") per topic per word
- Finally, we select the top-10 words with the highest weight, and collapse them to a single value for easy inspection (using the `.by` shortcut to skip the `group_by` step)

One small note: LDA is a 'mixture' model, which means that each document (and word) can be assigned to multiple topics. In our case this is not very useful since our documents are short sentences, but we can still use it to showcase the general working of LDA. 

::: {.challenge title="Playing with Topic Models"}
You can alter the code above to play around with the topic modeling algorithm. 

- What happens if you change the seed? Do you get similar clusters, or quite different. Note that the ordering of clusters is completely random, so even if you get similar clusters they will have different topic numbers. 
- What happens if you decrease k, e.g. to 2 or 5? Or increase it to 20? Do the topics feel more coherent, or less? Does their meaning shift?
:::

### Inspecting topic loadings {#sec-textasdata-lda-loadings}

Using similar code, we can also inspect the LDA topic loadings for each document, and compare it to the manually assigned topic:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_doc_topics', 'demo_topic_plot', 'demo_topic_sentences']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(topicmodels)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
dtm <- pimpo_en |>
  select(id:party, text, topic) |>
  unnest_tokens(input="text", output="word") |>
  anti_join(stop_words) |>
  count(id, word) |>
  cast_sparse(row=id, column=word, value=n)
t <- LDA(dtm, k=10, control=list(seed=99))
topic_terms <- posterior(t) |>
  pluck("terms") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "lda_topic") |>
  pivot_longer(-lda_topic, names_to = "term", values_to = "beta")
doc_topics <- posterior(t) |>
  pluck("topics") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "id") |>
  pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "lda_topic", values_to = "gamma") |>
  mutate(id = as.numeric(id)) |>
  left_join(pimpo_en, join_by(id))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_doc_topics
doc_topics <- posterior(t) |>
  pluck("topics") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "id") |>
  pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "lda_topic", values_to = "gamma") |>
  mutate(id = as.numeric(id)) |>
  left_join(pimpo_en, join_by(id))

doc_topics |>  
  summarize(gamma=mean(gamma), .by=c(lda_topic, topic)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = topic, y = factor(lda_topic, levels=1:10), fill = gamma)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(gamma, accuracy = 1))) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

The code here starts very similar to the earlier code, but plucking the `topics` from the posterior.
It then averages the 'gamma' weights per manual topic and LDA topic and uses that to create a heat map.
The gamma shows how each document is assigned to the various topics, so the columns add up to 100%.

This shows some interesting patterns. First, 
LDA topics 2 and 5 are most clearly related to immigration, but 1, 3 and 9 also each account for more than 10% of the immigration sentences.  
Integration peaks in topic 5, but this topic is shared with immigration and integration sentences are mostly spread over all the topics.
This is perhaps unsurprising given that our dictionary also had more difficulty finding sentences about integration. 
Finally, as we also saw in the top words, topic 10 is the clearest non-migration topic,
with 4, 7, and 8 also having more than 10% of 'other' sentences. 

The graph also shows that we should not read too much coherence into topics: 
the majority of immigration sentences ultimately ends up spread over other topics than 2 and 5.
This makes sense as immigration is often also discussed in its relation to other topics.
For example, looking at a number of immigration sentences from LDA topic 10, which we earlier saw contained *families* and *education*, it is clear that immigration is indeed also discussed in this context: keeping families together and the role of foreign talent. However, it also shows that topic 10 is much broader than just education, with many sentences talking about e.g. the rule of law. 
This highlights the importance of reading actual text to interpret topics rather than just looking at the top words, and avoiding the temptation to assume that a LDA topic maps perfectly on what we would normally call (political) topics. 

::: {.challenge title="Inspecting sentences"}

The code below shows the highest loading 'immigration' sentences for LDA topic 10:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_topic_sentences
doc_topics |>
  filter(lda_topic == "10", topic == "immigration") |>
  arrange(desc(gamma)) |>
  select(gamma, text)
```

- How would you evaluate and label the earlier 'families and education' topic (10) given these sentences?  Does it change if you look at sentences in the 'other' topic?
- For topic 5, have a look at both integration and immigration sentences in this topic. Does it make sense that these are combined in a single topic?
- Do other topics such as 2 or 9 make more sense? Can you find good labels for these topics?
:::


### Plotting words per topic {#sec-textasdata-lda-plot}


Finally, let's combine the document loadings with the word loadings to show the top words per topic, coded by how strongly the topic maps to an immigration topic:


```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_topic_plot
doc_topics |>
  slice_max(gamma, n = 1, by = id, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  summarize(perc_other = mean(topic == "other"), .by = lda_topic) |>
  inner_join(topic_terms, join_by(lda_topic)) |> 
  filter(lda_topic %in% c(3, 5, 9, 10)) |> 
  slice_max(beta, n = 8, by = lda_topic) |>
  mutate(term = reorder_within(term, beta, lda_topic)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = beta, y = term, fill = perc_other)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey70", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1), name = NULL,
                       breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1),
                       labels = c("immigration/\nintegration", "mixed", "other")) +
  facet_wrap(~lda_topic, scales = "free_y") + 
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.key.height = unit(2, "cm"))
```


This graph nicely showcases how hard it often is to interpret LDA topics.
Topic 10 is most strongly non-immigration related, with 'public' as the most prominent word and many words mentioning families, children, and schools. 
When you checked these sentences earlier in the challenge code, however,
you saw that it was a hotchpotch of various public policies, including education but also environmental concerns and public sector reforms.
Topic 5 is most clearly immigration-related, and seems to focus on enforcement and language. 
When we inspect the sentences in this topics, there seems to be a split with integration sentences focusing on language requirements, and immigration sentences focusing on border security and enforcement. 
Topics 3 and 9 both mix immigration and non-immigration sentences, with topic 9 focusing on asylum seekers and refugees and topic 3 containing many US-related words.

Looking at the code, we first take the top topic for each sentence, and
then compute the proportion of sentences in each LDA topic being in the handcoded 'other' topic
(note that slice_max uses `by=`, while summarize uses `.by=`). 
Then we join it with the `topic_terms` computed earlier,
select 4 interesting topics, and take the top 8 words for each topic.
We then use tidytext's `reorder_within` (and `scale_y_reordered`) to order the words by their loading within each topic, and create a faceted bar plot. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Is topic modeling still state of the art?"}

In the opening lines of this section I wrote that topic modeling "used to be a very popular method for exploring a corpus" -- which raises the question of its current status in the methodological toolbox. 

The short answer is that it is still somewhat useful for a quick exploration of a corpus,
but has lost most of its use as an analytical tool. 

The reason for this is possibly that it never quite delivered on its 'promise' of finding topics in documents. As the demo above showed, many LDA topics don't neatly correspond to what we would call topics.
The output is also hard to validate if you don't know what topics you are interested in before the analysis [but see @chang2009reading]. And if you do have hand coded topics, such as in our PImPo data set,
the correlation of LDA topics with manually coded topics is often relatively weak:
Even if we take topics 2, 3, 5 and 9 together, these topics still only contain about 57% of all immigration sentences, and even the most clearly immigration/integration related topic (5) still only has a precision of 72% while finding only 15% of sentences. 
These numbers are clearly worse even than the small dictionary used above -- at 57% recall, precision drops to 62%, against 99% precision for a dictionary with similar recall. 
Note that this is not a fault in the method, but rather underscores that LDA topic modeling is not a
very useful technique for finding specific topics known beforehand, but rather for exploring an unknown corpus. 

In @sec-embeddings we will explore a more modern approach to word clustering using *embeddings*, 
which have the benefit of re-using linguistic and pragmatic knowledge from existing language models,
so the clustering does not have to 'discover' that e.g. *immigration* and *migrant* are related terms. 

If you do want to use regular topic modeling, it is a good idea to check out Structural Topic Models [@roberts2014structural], which allow specifying covariates such as country or year to affect the topic loadings. 
:::
